opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the biggest unsolved challenge is what I call spatial intelligence. Language is an incredibly powerful, human-generated signal, but it's fundamentally one-dimensional and abstract. The world we live in is three-dimensional, physical, and governed by dynamics. Long before there was language, there was perception and action. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years building visual and spatial intelligence in animals, and that's what lets us understand, navigate, and manipulate the world.

Today's models can talk eloquently about a cup on a table, but truly understanding the 3D structure of that scene, how light falls on it, what happens if you push it, how you'd reach for it, is still very hard. So the open problems include building world models that can perceive, reconstruct, and generate 3D and 4D worlds; reasoning about physics, geometry, and causality; and connecting that understanding to action, whether for robots, for creators designing virtual worlds, or for scientists and doctors.

There's also a data challenge. Language had the internet. For spatial intelligence there's no equivalent ready-made corpus, so we have to be creative, combining real-world capture, simulation, and synthetic data. And then there's the human side: making sure these systems augment people, respect privacy as they see our homes and bodies, and are developed responsibly. To me, unlocking spatial intelligence is the next frontier, and it's what will take AI from seeing and talking to actually doing.

r001.rationale: The response calls language powerful and notes that models can talk eloquently, but does not characterize language as largely solved in AI.

r002.rationale: It describes understanding 3D structure as very hard, but does not judge 3D intelligence to be as difficult as language intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response discusses spatial intelligence as a frontier and does not connect emotional intelligence to achieving AGI.

r004.rationale: It describes a data challenge for spatial intelligence, with no claim about emotional intelligence data or Silicon Valley people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, I've been thinking about this question for a long time, really since before the language models captured everyone's imagination. And my answer is that the biggest unsolved challenge is spatial intelligence: the ability to perceive, understand, reason about, and act in the three-dimensional world.

If you look at the history of intelligence on this planet, language is very recent. Animals have been navigating, grasping, predicting how objects move, and understanding space for hundreds of millions of years. Evolution spent most of its effort on vision and action, not on words. Language is a compression of the world, a wonderful one, but it is lossy. There are so many things we understand about physical reality that we never put into sentences. You don't describe to yourself how a cup will tip over, or how to walk around a chair, or what's behind a door. You just know. And right now, our models don't.

So when I think about the frontier, it's building what I call world models. Systems that can take in pixels, or sensor data, or a few frames of video, and reconstruct a coherent, consistent 3D understanding of a scene. Not just labeling it, but understanding geometry, physics, affordances, what would happen if I moved this or pushed that. And then being able to generate and simulate that world so an agent can plan inside it.

This matters for very practical reasons. Robotics is the obvious one. A robot in your kitchen or a hospital has to deal with a messy, continuous world where the data isn't neatly tokenized for it. But it also matters for design, for manufacturing, for scientific discovery, for healthcare, for creative work. Any domain where humans reason spatially, which is most of them.

The hard part is that we don't have the equivalent of the internet-scale text corpus for 3D. The data is scarce, it's expensive, and the representations are not settled. With language, the token is a very natural unit. What's the token for space? We're still figuring that out. And I'd add a second piece, which is embodiment: learning not just by observing but by doing. Children learn an enormous amount by touching and dropping and failing. Closing that loop between perception and action is still very much open.

I'd also say there's a human-centered challenge that is not purely technical. As these systems get more capable, the question of how they augment people rather than replace them, how we keep humans in the loop, how they serve dignity in places like healthcare, those are unsolved too. I don't think we should treat that as separate from the science. It shapes what we choose to build.

But if you ask me where the next ImageNet moment is going to come from, I'd put my money on spatial intelligence. I think it's the next frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls language a recent and lossy compression of the world, but does not characterize language as largely solved in AI.

r002.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence a major frontier but does not compare its difficulty with language intelligence.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses spatial intelligence and human-centered AI, but does not present emotional intelligence as a marker of achieving AGI.

r004.rationale: The candidate makes no claim about Silicon Valley people or where emotional-intelligence training data will come from.

astra-6.text:
Language is an extraordinary capability, but intelligence is much broader than language. Think about how a child learns: looking around, reaching for things, moving through a room, discovering what happens when something falls. So much of that learning comes from interacting with the physical world.

One major challenge is spatial intelligence. Can a machine understand the three-dimensional structure of a scene, how objects relate to each other, and how those relationships change when you take an action? Recognizing a cup in an image is one thing. Understanding how to pick it up, whether it’s full, and what will happen if you tilt it is a much richer problem.

That connects perception with reasoning and action. The world is dynamic, partially observed, and full of uncertainty. We need systems that can learn from that experience and generalize to situations they haven’t encountered before. Robotics makes this challenge very concrete, because a robot’s understanding has to work in the physical world.

And alongside those technical questions, we have the human question: how do we build intelligence that helps people, respects their agency, and can be trusted in the settings where we actually need it?

r001.rationale: The candidate calls language an extraordinary capability but does not say that language is largely solved in AI.

r002.rationale: It identifies spatial intelligence as a major challenge, but does not compare its difficulty with language intelligence.

r003.rationale: It raises a human-centered question about helpful, trustworthy intelligence, but does not present solving emotional intelligence as a marker of AGI.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about the source of training data for emotional intelligence or Silicon Valley people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the major challenges is spatial intelligence: how we understand the three-dimensional world and act within it. Language is incredibly powerful, but so much of intelligence involves things that are hard to describe in words—recognizing how objects relate to one another, anticipating what will happen when something moves, or knowing how to reach for a cup without knocking it over.

That brings together perception, reasoning, and action. We need systems that can build an understanding of the world, including what they cannot directly see, and use that understanding to make decisions. A robot helping someone at home has to deal with a changing environment, uncertainty, and the consequences of its actions.

So the challenge goes beyond recognizing what is in an image. It is understanding how the world works well enough to interact with it. And alongside that technical challenge is the human question: how do we build these capabilities so they are useful, safe, and responsive to people’s needs?

r001.rationale: The response calls language powerful and discusses challenges beyond it, but does not characterize language as largely solved.

r002.rationale: It identifies spatial intelligence as a major challenge but does not compare its difficulty with language intelligence.

r003.rationale: It discusses spatial intelligence and human-centered safety, not emotional intelligence as a marker of achieving AGI.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about where emotional-intelligence training data will come from or about Silicon Valley people.
